records.statement: Russell's comment in the 2019 thread states that in a toy decision problem an agent rewarded only for fetching coffee would switch off a human who might switch it off, with no built-in survival instinct or desire for power.

time.note: Dated by the LessWrong copy of 4 October 2019. The Facebook thread follows the Scientific American piece of 26 September 2019; the copy gives no date for individual comments.

attested.note: The wording is known from the LessWrong copy, whose compiler states that he improved formatting and fixed typos; the Facebook original was not compared.

records.qualification: A toy model offered as a mathematical observation, for a single specified reward (fetching coffee); the generalisation to almost any goal is stated in the question that opens the thread, not in Russell's comment. Each comment is the participant's own words in a relayed copy; the record states what the comment says in this thread, not the author's view at another date.

evidence.passage: the agent will necessarily press that button as part of the optimal solution for fetching the coffee. No hatred, no desire for power, no built-in emotions, no built-in survival instinct, nothing except the desire to fetch the coffee successfully.

records.statement: Russell's comment in the 2019 thread states that machines are already built on the assumption of a fixed, known objective, that this becomes more untenable as they become more powerful, and that there is no hope of solving value alignment by specifying the right value function offline.

time.note: Dated by the LessWrong copy of 4 October 2019. The Facebook thread follows the Scientific American piece of 26 September 2019; the copy gives no date for individual comments.

attested.note: The wording is known from the LessWrong copy, whose compiler states that he improved formatting and fixed typos; the Facebook original was not compared.

records.qualification: States the difficulty for the standard model of AI and argues for changing it; not a claim that alignment cannot be achieved in any way. Each comment is the participant's own words in a relayed copy; the record states what the comment says in this thread, not the author's view at another date.

evidence.locator: Comment Thread #2, Stuart Russell (reply to Francesca Rossi)
evidence.passage: There is no hope of "solving the value alignment problem" in the sense of figuring out the right value function offline and putting it into the machine. We need to change the way we do AI.

records.statement: LeCun's comments in the 2019 thread argue that the instrumental drives Russell describes are avoided by safeguard terms in a system's objective, and that instrumental subgoals are much weaker drives of behaviour than hardwired objectives.

time.note: Dated by the LessWrong copy of 4 October 2019. The Facebook thread follows the Scientific American piece of 26 September 2019; the copy gives no date for individual comments.

attested.note: The wording is known from the LessWrong copy, whose compiler states that he improved formatting and fixed typos; the Facebook original was not compared.

engagement.rationale: Gives reasons against the premise that instrumental subgoals would drive a built system's behaviour: safeguard terms can be added to the objective, and instrumental subgoals are weaker than hardwired objectives.

records.qualification: Contests the conclusion that instrumental subgoals would make such behaviour likely in systems as they would be built. Each comment is the participant's own words in a relayed copy; the record states what the comment says in this thread, not the author's view at another date.

evidence.locator: Comment Thread #2, Yann LeCun (reply to Stuart Russell)
evidence.passage: The point is that behaviors you are concerned about are easily avoidable by simple terms in the objective.
instrumental subgoals are much weaker drives of behavior than hardwired objectives.

records.statement: LeCun's comments in the 2019 thread state that it will be much easier to control the behaviour of autonomous AI systems than that of humans and human organisations, because their intrinsic objective function can be modified directly.

time.note: Dated by the LessWrong copy of 4 October 2019. The Facebook thread follows the Scientific American piece of 26 September 2019; the copy gives no date for individual comments.

attested.note: The wording is known from the LessWrong copy, whose compiler states that he improved formatting and fixed typos; the Facebook original was not compared.

records.qualification: Each comment is the participant's own words in a relayed copy; the record states what the comment says in this thread, not the author's view at another date.

evidence.passage: It will be much, much easier to control the behavior of autonomous AI systems than it has been for humans and human organizations, because we will be able to directly modify their intrinsic objective function.

records.statement: LeCun's comments in the 2019 thread state that he disagrees that there is a high risk of accidentally building existential threats to humanity, holding that such threats have to be designed as such.

time.note: Dated by the LessWrong copy of 4 October 2019. The Facebook thread follows the Scientific American piece of 26 September 2019; the copy gives no date for individual comments.

attested.note: The wording is known from the LessWrong copy, whose compiler states that he improved formatting and fixed typos; the Facebook original was not compared.

engagement.rationale: States the contrary conclusion (existential threats must be designed) without a further argument in this comment; the reasons are given in his other comments on R02 and R10b.

records.qualification: Contests the accidental, unintended route the criterion describes. Each comment is the participant's own words in a relayed copy; the record states what the comment says in this thread, not the author's view at another date.

evidence.locator: Comment Thread #2, Yann LeCun (reply to Stuart Russell)
evidence.passage: But I disagree that there is a high risk of accidentally building existential threats to humanity. Existential threats to humanity have to be explicitly designed as such.

records.statement: Zador's comments in the 2019 thread argue that for a robot that is not omnipotent, killing humans carries the risk of retaliation, so that it is unlikely to be an optimal strategy in most scenarios.

time.note: Dated by the LessWrong copy of 4 October 2019. The Facebook thread follows the Scientific American piece of 26 September 2019; the copy gives no date for individual comments.

attested.note: The wording is known from the LessWrong copy, whose compiler states that he improved formatting and fixed typos; the Facebook original was not compared.

engagement.rationale: Gives a reason against the premise that eliminating a threat is the optimal subgoal: for a non-omnipotent agent it invites retaliation, and other strategies serve survival.

records.qualification: Contests the claim that harming humans would be an instrumentally optimal strategy, not that instrumental goals exist. Each comment is the participant's own words in a relayed copy; the record states what the comment says in this thread, not the author's view at another date.

evidence.passage: killing all humans is not only not likely to be an optimal strategy under most scenarios, the set of scenarios under which it is optimal is probably close to a set of measure 0.

records.statement: Zador's comment in the 2019 thread states that focusing on killer robots that dominate humans is a distraction from much more serious issues, which he presents as the unintended societal consequences that improvements in AI will have, by analogy with books, food production technology and social media.

time.note: Dated by the LessWrong copy of 4 October 2019. The Facebook thread follows the Scientific American piece of 26 September 2019; the copy gives no date for individual comments.

attested.note: The wording is known from the LessWrong copy, whose compiler states that he improved formatting and fixed typos; the Facebook original was not compared.

records.missing: Documented present harms of AI systems: the serious issues are unforeseen future consequences of AI, illustrated by other technologies.
records.qualification: In the same comment Zador states that value alignment is important and not a solved problem. Each comment is the participant's own words in a relayed copy; the record states what the comment says in this thread, not the author's view at another date.

evidence.locator: Comment Thread #2, Tony Zador (reply to Yoshua Bengio)
evidence.passage: But in my view, focusing on "killer robots that dominate or step on humans" is a distraction from much more serious issues.

records.statement: Bengio's comments in the 2019 thread state that even if rogue AI from value misalignment can be mitigated, a single person acting greedily for power could unleash dangerous AIs, and that the misalignment of powerful people or companies with the common good can lead to catastrophic outcomes.

time.note: Dated by the LessWrong copy of 4 October 2019. The Facebook thread follows the Scientific American piece of 26 September 2019; the copy gives no date for individual comments.

attested.note: The wording is known from the LessWrong copy, whose compiler states that he improved formatting and fixed typos; the Facebook original was not compared.

records.qualification: Raised as a further concern beside misalignment, without ranking the two. Each comment is the participant's own words in a relayed copy; the record states what the comment says in this thread, not the author's view at another date.

evidence.passage: how can we guarantee that no single human will act stupidly (more likely, greedily for their own power) and unleash dangerous AIs in the world? And for this, we don't even need superintelligent AIs, to feel very concerned.

records.statement: Bengio's comments in the 2019 thread agree that machines' objectives can be designed and trained, and state that AI systems surpassing human intellectual power could foil attempts at setting objectives that avoid harm, which calls for more research on value alignment.

time.note: Dated by the LessWrong copy of 4 October 2019. The Facebook thread follows the Scientific American piece of 26 September 2019; the copy gives no date for individual comments.

attested.note: The wording is known from the LessWrong copy, whose compiler states that he improved formatting and fixed typos; the Facebook original was not compared.

engagement.rationale: Gives a reason against the premise that designing a system's objective keeps it controllable: a system more capable than its designers could foil the objectives set for it.

records.qualification: Bengio states the possibility as one that is hard to deny, not as a forecast, and says it is probably not near. Each comment is the participant's own words in a relayed copy; the record states what the comment says in this thread, not the author's view at another date.

evidence.locator: Comment Thread #2, Yoshua Bengio (reply to Yann LeCun)
evidence.passage: there could be AI systems which surpass human intellectual power in ways that could foil our attempts at setting objective functions which avoid harm to us.

replies.statement: LeCun's comment in the 2019 thread replies to Russell's coffee-fetching argument, which Bengio had asked him to answer.
replies.qualification: A reply is not agreement; it records that the comment addresses the other participant.

evidence.passage: You mean, the so-called "instrumental convergence" argument by which "a robot can't fetch you coffee if it's dead.

replies.statement: Zador's comment in the 2019 thread replies to Russell's argument, naming him.
replies.qualification: A reply is not agreement; it records that the comment addresses the other participant.

evidence.passage: I think the flaw in Stuart's argument is the assertion that "switching off the human is the optimal solution"

replies.statement: Russell's comment in the 2019 thread replies to Zador's.
replies.qualification: A reply is not agreement; it records that the comment addresses the other participant.

evidence.passage: I simply pointed out that in the MDP as I defined it, switching off the human is the optimal solution

replies.statement: Bengio's comment in the 2019 thread replies to LeCun's points on designing objectives.
replies.qualification: A reply is not agreement; it records that the comment addresses the other participant.

evidence.locator: Comment Thread #2, Yoshua Bengio (reply to Yann LeCun)
evidence.passage: Yann, these are good points, we indeed have much more control over machines than humans since we can design (and train) their objective function.

replies.statement: LeCun's comment in the 2019 thread replies to Bengio's summary of the debate.
replies.qualification: A reply is not agreement; it records that the comment addresses the other participant.

evidence.passage: @Yoshua Bengio a couple direct comments on your summary
